t10.triage:
*When:* Any timed mixed set where you cannot finish every question at full effort.

*Why:* Each question is worth the same, but not each costs the same. Easy points left unread because you sank time into one hard item are lost for nothing.

*Move:*
$$\text{time per question}=\frac{\text{total time}}{\text{questions}}$$
Make a first pass and answer every question you can see through in under a minute. Mark anything that stalls after about thirty seconds, and move on. Return to the marked ones in order of how close you were. Guess before time runs out.

*Example:* A set has $20$ questions in $50$ minutes.
$$\frac{50}{20}=2.5\text{ min each},\qquad \text{first pass: }12\text{ solved in }15\text{ min}$$
That leaves $35$ minutes for the $8$ marked questions, about $4$ minutes each.

*Trap:* Spending five minutes on one derivation that a second look later would solve in one.

*Check:* After the first pass, the time left per marked question should exceed the time per question at the start.
t10.plug-choices:
*When:* A multiple-choice question has a number or formula answer and a long derivation looks likely.

*Why:* The correct answer is among the options. Testing options often takes less work than solving, and one failed test removes a choice for good.

*Move:*
$$\text{substitute option }x_i\text{ into the condition; keep it only if both sides agree}$$
Start with the simplest numbers or the middle value. Plug each option into the stated equation. Discard the ones that fail. If two options survive, test them at a second input.

*Example:* Which $x$ satisfies $2^x+2^{x+1}=24$, from the options $2,3,4,5$?
$$x=3:\ 8+16=24\ \checkmark,\qquad x=2:\ 4+8=12\ \times$$
So $x=3$, found without taking logarithms.

*Trap:* Trusting one test when two options pass it.

*Check:* The chosen option must satisfy every condition in the question, not just the first one you tried.
t10.special-cases:
*When:* Options contain a parameter such as $n$, or a matrix or symmetric setup, and the general proof is long.

*Why:* A true formula holds in every special case. If an option gives the wrong value in one case, that option is false.

*Move:*
$$\text{true value at a simple case}\ \ne\ \text{option at that case}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{discard}$$
Choose $n=1$ or $n=2$, the identity matrix, or a symmetric configuration where the answer is known. Compute the true value there. Evaluate every option at the same case and cross off those that disagree.

*Example:* The sum $1+2+\cdots+n$ is offered as $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, $\frac{n^2}{2}$, or $n^2$.
$$n=1:\ \text{true }1;\quad \frac{1\cdot2}2=1\ \checkmark,\ \ \frac12\ \times,\ \ 1\ \checkmark$$
Test $n=2$, where the true value is $3$ and the last option gives $4$.

*Trap:* Choosing a case so special, like zero, that wrong options also pass.

*Check:* Use two different cases before you commit.
t10.sanity-check:
*When:* You have just derived an answer, or picked one, and a few seconds remain before moving on.

*Why:* Most wrong answers break a basic fact. A quick test of that fact catches slips that a rerun of the algebra repeats.

*Move:*
$$\text{units, sign, size, limits, and trend of the answer}$$
Ask five questions. Do the units match the quantity asked? Is the sign plausible? Is the size reasonable? Does it behave correctly when a parameter goes to $0$ or grows large? Does it move the right way as an input increases?

*Example:* A candidate for the average speed over two equal legs at $30$ and $60$ is $45$. Check the size.
$$\text{the true value is the harmonic mean }\frac{2\cdot30\cdot60}{30+60}=40$$
The slower leg takes more time, so the average must sit below the midpoint $45$. A candidate of $45$ is suspect.

*Trap:* Treating a passed check as proof. It only rules out errors.

*Check:* Run at least two of the five tests, in under ten seconds.
t10.time-boxing:
*When:* A test is timed and you are working through it question by question.

*Why:* A fixed pace turns drift into a visible number. You notice early when you are behind, while there is still time to adjust.

*Move:*
$$\text{budget}=\frac{\text{total minutes}}{\text{questions}},\qquad \text{checkpoint at half the time}$$
Set a budget per question before you start. At the halfway mark compare the question count with the plan. If you are behind, drop to faster methods and skip sooner. Leave the last minutes for guessing every blank.

*Example:* A test has $40$ questions in $100$ minutes.
$$\frac{100}{40}=2.5\text{ min},\qquad \text{checkpoint: question }20\text{ by minute }50$$
At question $16$ by minute $50$, speed up by skipping anything not started within thirty seconds.

*Trap:* Spending the last ten minutes on one hard question while easy ones stay blank.

*Check:* The number of questions you have seen should match the clock at each checkpoint.
